extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy of science, and general reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Analyse the nature and functions of syllogisms, generalization, and induction — distinguishing inference-from-particulars from the registering/interpretive role of syllogistic forms. Emphasizes when general propositions are merely shorthand and how generalization secures and tests inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitio principii in every syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be granted that in every syllogism, considered as an argument to prove the conclusion, there is a petitio principii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the adversary's objection that the conclusion (e.g. 'Socrates is mortal') is presupposed by the general premise ('All men are mortal'), so no reasoning from generals to particulars can, as such, prove anything beyond what the premises already involve. Use this criterion to check whether a syllogism merely restates an assumed conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish inferring vs registering parts of philosophizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlooking the distinction between two parts of the process of philosophizing, the inferring part, and the registering part, is an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The registering part (memoranda, general propositions) records past inferences; the inferring part is where knowledge actually arises. Evaluation should separate whether a given syllogistic form represents the original act of inference or merely the subsequent recording/decoding of that inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference originates in particulars (induction from observed instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: All which man can observe are individual cases. From these all general truths must be drawn, and into these they may be again resolved; for a general truth is but an aggregate of particular truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat general propositions as compressions of observed particulars plus the inferences drawn from them. When judging an argument, ask whether the supposed general premise was actually produced by sufficient particular observations (induction), since particulars are the real evidential basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism is a means of interpretation, not the true analysis of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Though there is always a process of reasoning or inference where a syllogism is used, the syllogism is not a correct analysis of that process of reasoning or inference; the syllogistic form is the latter half (registering/interpretation), not the originating inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the syllogistic form as a tool to interpret memoranda or authorities (decoding what was intended), not as the claim that the deduction itself happened from the general to the particular. The rules of syllogism serve as 'precautions' to ensure correct reading of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions are registers and short-form rules for inference
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions are merely registers of such inferences already made, and short formulæ for making more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, regard general statements as shorthand prescriptions summarizing past particular inferences and guiding future ones. This reframes the major premise as an operational formula rather than as an independent evidential source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of generalization as a security/test for inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: This throwing of the whole body of possible inferences from a given set of particulars into one general expression operates as a security for their being just inferences, in more ways than one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include: (a) the general principle presents a larger object to imagination prompting more careful scrutiny of evidence, and (b) it allows reductio-style checks — if the generalization would imply known false cases, the premises are insufficient. Apply this standard when deciding whether to reframe an individual inference as a general proposition to test its robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonness of reasoning from particulars to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: We much oftener conclude from particulars to particulars directly, than through the intermediate agency of any general proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and evaluate direct particular-to-particular inferences (e.g., child burned avoids flame) as legitimate forms of reasoning, especially in practical/intuitive contexts. Do not demand explicit general formulæ where skilled practice or stored particulars suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and definitions function as shorthand for particular assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The general propositions, whether called definitions, axioms, or laws of nature, which we lay down at the beginning of our reasonings, are merely abridged statements, in a kind of short-hand, of the particular facts, which ... we either think we may proceed on as proved, or intend to assume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing mathematical or scientific demonstrations, note that diagrams and particular assumptions can suffice for conviction even when axioms/definitions are not explicitly invoked; axioms are necessary in general form only when proving all cases at once. Use this to judge whether appeal to an axiom is substantive or merely notational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic rules maintain consistency between particular conclusions and prior general directions
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole purpose [of the syllogism] is to maintain consistency between the conclusions we draw in every particular case, and the previous general directions for drawing them; whether those general directions were framed by ourselves as the result of induction, or were received by us from an authority competent to give them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments for internal consistency: if one accepts a general rule (induced or authoritative), one should not draw particular conclusions that contradict that rule. Use syllogistic rules as consistency-checking procedures rather than as independent sources of new evidential content.

rubrics_metrics.name: When premises come from authority, reasoning is interpretation (hermeneutics)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the premises are given by authority, the function of Reasoning is to ascertain the testimony of a witness, or the will of a legislator, by interpreting the signs in which the one has intimated his assertion and the other his command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating deductions from authoritative generalities (testimony, laws, scriptures), treat the process as hermeneutic: determine whether the authoritative statement was intended to include the present particular. Apply interpretive rules rather than treating the syllogism as purely inductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascend to general propositions when judging contested inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: In arguing from a number of known cases to another case supposed to be analogous, it is always possible, and generally advantageous, to divert our argument into the circuitous channel of an induction from those known cases to a general proposition, and a subsequent application of that general proposition to the unknown case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with disputed analogical reasoning, reframe the argument as an induction to a general rule and then apply that rule; doing so often reveals insufficiencies in the evidence (via counterexamples) and thus serves as a diagnostic method for legitimacy of the original inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: State inductions in their broadest generality to expose weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Every induction, therefore, which suffices to prove one fact, proves an indefinite multitude of facts: the experience which justifies a single prediction must be such as will suffice to bear out a general theorem. This theorem it is extremely important to ascertain and declare, in its broadest form of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating an induction, articulate the general theorem it supports in the broadest clear form; doing so increases scrutiny and helps detect counterexamples or absurd implications (illustrated by the Commodus/Nero example). This is an advised best-practice for robust induction.
